blocks.content: A group can help you settle into a race, but the draft is not worth riding into a wheel or a hole you could not see. Keep enough room to choose your own line on rough ground. There is no universal wheel gap or power percentage for every surface.

blocks.label: Space to see and respond
blocks.content: When you follow another rider, look through and around the group instead of staring at the tire in front of you. You should have room to avoid a visible obstacle without overlapping wheels or grabbing the brakes. If the surface hides hazards, make the gap larger or ride separately.

### The useful part of a group

Drafting can reduce effort on a steady, open road. Rough gravel changes the trade. Riders choose different lines, stand for bumps, and slow at different moments. The rider ahead may block your view of a rut or loose patch. The right gap is the one that lets you see, react, and avoid overlapping a wheel. It changes with speed, visibility, surface, and the riders around you.

On a group ride, say what you are doing. Point or call out a hazard when it is safe to do so, pass predictably, and leave space before moving back into line. If the group cannot ride smoothly through a rough section, let it go and find your own line.

items.title: Why a fixed drafting number fails
items.content:
Aerodynamic benefit changes with speed, wind, position, and separation. None of those tells you the stopping room you need when the road turns rough. A precise promise that one gap saves a set number of watts can hide the more important question: can you still see and steer around a hazard?

Use drafting where the surface and group are predictable. On loose or broken ground, spend the extra space needed for visibility and independent line choice.

blocks.content:
### Pace by the work you can sustain

A power meter tells you what you are producing at the pedals. It does not tell you whether the next sandy section, climb, or group surge is worth that effort. If traction is poor, forcing a big gear can spin the rear wheel. Shift easier, keep your pedal stroke smooth, and let speed vary with the surface.

On firm ground, return to the effort you planned for the whole ride. Do not chase a fixed FTP percentage just because a chart calls the surface efficient. Eat, drink, and reassess what you can hold as the day changes. The goal is to finish with enough control to keep riding your own bike.

blocks.title: The Elastic Gap
blocks.description: A group-riding check for mixed surfaces. The gap can open without ending your ride.

steps.detail: Scan the road beyond the wheel directly ahead.
Avoid overlapping wheels. Open the gap when the road gets rough, narrow, or hard to read.
Freewheel or brake gently rather than grabbing a lever at the last moment.
Shift to a gear that lets you pedal smoothly without spinning the rear tire.
If riders make unpredictable moves or block every safe line, create space and ride your own pace.

blocks.title: Space and Sightline Check
blocks.description: Practice on a quiet, familiar route with a willing partner. Stay at a conversational pace; this is a visibility exercise, not close drafting. A solo rider can observe the same sightline changes from different positions on a traffic-free path.

variants.label: With a partner
steps: Agree on the route, pace, calls, and where you will stop before starting.
Ride behind at a gap that lets you see the surface ahead and choose your own line.
On a rougher section, open the gap until you can identify hazards without following the exact wheel track.
Stop in a safe place and compare what each of you could see. Do not shorten the gap to prove a drafting gain.

variants.label: Without a partner
steps: On a quiet, familiar route, notice how a rise, bend, or roadside feature changes what you can see.
Choose a pace that lets you stop within the visible space and identify where you would make room for another rider.
Record the section where you would need more space in a group.

proof_gate.description: You can describe when a group blocks your view and how you will create room.
proof_gate.target: Record one surface or sightline that requires more spacing; no fixed wheel gap

blocks.question: A group speeds up as the route turns onto loose, broken gravel. You can no longer see a clear line around the rider ahead. What is the best choice?

options.text: Open the gap, choose your own line, and ride an effort you can sustain
Close onto the wheel because the draft always outweighs the risk
Overlap the wheel ahead so you can see around that rider
Match the surge at any power needed to stay attached

blocks.explanation: Visibility and independent line choice matter on rough ground. Let the gap open and use smooth, predictable inputs. You can regroup when the surface and group settle.

blocks.content: On your next group ride, note one place where more space improved your view or line choice. If you ride solo, note where a group would have blocked your sightline. Write down how you would adjust.
